subtopic_detail: An anti-Kell antibody titre of 1 in 16 at twenty weeks with a partner heterozygous for the Kell antigen
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 31 year old woman at 20 weeks in her second pregnancy. Her antibody screen at booking detected anti-Kell, and the repeat titre today is 1 in 16.

She received two units of red cells after a retained placenta in her first pregnancy, and that baby was well with no jaundice. Her blood group is O RhD positive, so anti-D is not relevant to her care. Genotyping shows her partner is heterozygous for the Kell antigen, and cell free foetal DNA testing reports the foetus as Kell antigen positive. The anatomy ultrasound today is structurally normal with no ascites, no skin oedema and a normal amniotic fluid volume.

data_table.Examination: Symphysis fundal height 20 cm consistent with dates, foetal movements reported as normal, no abdominal tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Maternal blood group O RhD positive, antibody screen positive for anti-Kell with a titre of 1 in 16, paternal genotype heterozygous for the Kell antigen, cell free foetal DNA reports the foetus as Kell antigen positive, anatomy ultrasound structurally normal with no ascites or skin oedema and normal amniotic fluid volume

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for foetal surveillance?

options.text: Repeat the antibody titre monthly and intervene when it reaches 1 in 32
options.rationale: Titres correlate poorly with the severity of foetal anaemia for this antibody, because the mechanism is suppression of erythroid precursors rather than haemolysis of circulating cells, so a modest titre can accompany severe anaemia. Referral thresholds for this antibody are accordingly lower than for anti-D and titre alone does not guide timing. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal red cell alloimmunisation)

options.text: Arrange serial amniocentesis for amniotic fluid bilirubin from 24 weeks
options.rationale: Amniotic fluid bilirubin measurement assumes anaemia is produced by haemolysis, which generates the bilirubin being measured, and it therefore underestimates severity when the mechanism is marrow suppression. It has in any case been superseded by non invasive Doppler assessment, which avoids the procedure related risks. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal red cell alloimmunisation)

options.text: Give anti-D immunoglobulin at 28 and 34 weeks and continue routine care
options.rationale: Anti-D immunoglobulin prevents sensitisation to the RhD antigen only, and this woman is RhD positive with an antibody to a different red cell antigen entirely. There is no immunoglobulin preparation that prevents or treats sensitisation to this antigen. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal red cell alloimmunisation)

options.text: Plan delivery at 37 weeks with no additional antenatal surveillance
options.rationale: Severe foetal anaemia and hydrops can develop well before term, so a delivery plan without surveillance leaves a treatable condition undetected in the interim. Intrauterine transfusion in the second and third trimesters is what prevents that outcome. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Haemolytic disease of the newborn)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Haemolytic disease of the newborn

options.text: Refer for serial middle cerebral artery Doppler velocity surveillance
options.rationale: With an antigen positive foetus confirmed, surveillance is by serial middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity in a foetal medicine unit, since a value above 1.5 multiples of the median predicts moderate to severe anaemia and triggers foetal blood sampling with intrauterine transfusion. This non invasive measure is particularly important for this antibody because the titre is an unreliable guide to severity. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal red cell alloimmunisation)

explanation.summary: Red cell alloimmunisation is no longer dominated by anti-D since routine prophylaxis, so antibodies such as anti-Kell, anti-c and anti-E now account for much of the serious disease seen in practice. Anti-Kell is distinctive because the antigen is expressed on erythroid progenitors, so the antibody suppresses red cell production in the foetal marrow in addition to causing haemolysis, and the result is anaemia with comparatively little bilirubin production. That mechanism explains two practical consequences: maternal titres and amniotic fluid bilirubin both underestimate severity, and referral thresholds for this antibody are set lower than for anti-D. Management therefore rests on establishing the foetal antigen status, by cell free foetal DNA where available or by paternal genotyping, and then on serial middle cerebral artery Doppler in a unit able to perform intrauterine transfusion.
key_points: The antigen is expressed on erythroid precursors, so marrow suppression occurs
Titres correlate poorly with severity for this antibody
Amniotic fluid bilirubin underestimates anaemia when haemolysis is not the mechanism
A heterozygous partner means the foetal antigen status must be determined
Peak systolic velocity above 1.5 multiples of the median triggers intervention
explanation.pearls: Because anti-Kell suppresses erythropoiesis rather than simply destroying circulating cells, an affected foetus can be severely anaemic with a maternal titre as low as 1 in 8, which is why that titre rather than the 1 in 32 used for anti-D is the usual referral threshold.

sources.label: National Blood Authority: Guidelines on the prophylactic use of Rh D immunoglobulin
BMJ Best Practice: Haemolytic disease of the newborn

subtopic_detail: Immunoglobulin M positive and immunoglobulin G negative parvovirus serology at sixteen weeks in a childcare worker exposed to slapped cheek rash
stem:
You are the obstetrician seeing a 30 year old childcare worker at 16 weeks in her second pregnancy. Three weeks ago several children in her room developed a bright red rash on both cheeks, and a fortnight ago she had two days of aching joints in her hands and a mild fever that she put down to a virus.

She feels well now and reports normal foetal movements for her gestation. She asks whether the outbreak at work could harm the baby. Her serology taken this week reports immunoglobulin M positive and immunoglobulin G negative for parvovirus B19, with rubella immunoglobulin G immune and cytomegalovirus immunoglobulin G positive from booking. An ultrasound today shows a structurally normal foetus with no ascites, no pericardial effusion, no skin oedema and normal amniotic fluid.

data_table.Examination: Symphysis fundal height consistent with dates, no rash or joint swelling currently, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Parvovirus B19 immunoglobulin M positive and immunoglobulin G negative, rubella immunoglobulin G immune, cytomegalovirus immunoglobulin G positive from booking bloods, full blood count within normal limits, ultrasound shows a structurally normal foetus with no ascites, no pericardial effusion, no skin oedema and normal amniotic fluid volume

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Reassure her and continue routine antenatal care without extra surveillance
options.rationale: Recent maternal infection at this gestation carries a real risk of foetal anaemia and hydrops over the following weeks, and a single normal scan at the time of diagnosis does not exclude it developing later. The risk window is the reason surveillance is time limited rather than absent. (Source: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 in pregnancy)

options.text: Offer termination of pregnancy because of the risk of foetal abnormality
options.rationale: This virus does not cause a congenital malformation syndrome, and the foetal risk is a treatable anaemia rather than structural damage, with the great majority of pregnancies proceeding normally. Offering termination misrepresents the prognosis. (Source: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 in pregnancy)

options.text: Arrange weekly ultrasound for foetal anaemia and hydrops for twelve weeks
options.rationale: Serial ultrasound with middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity, performed weekly for 8 to 12 weeks after maternal infection, detects developing anaemia at a stage when intrauterine transfusion can be given and hydrops reversed. Surveillance is time limited because the risk is concentrated in that interval and falls away afterwards. (Source: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 in pregnancy)

options.text: Give intravenous immunoglobulin to the mother and continue routine care
options.rationale: There is no evidence that maternal immunoglobulin prevents foetal infection or anaemia with this virus, and it would replace the surveillance that actually changes outcome. The effective intervention is transfusion of the foetus once anaemia is detected. (Source: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 in pregnancy)

options.text: Arrange amniocentesis for viral nucleic acid testing and then reassess
options.rationale: Confirming that the foetus is infected does not alter management, because treatment is triggered by anaemia rather than by infection, and amniocentesis carries a procedure related loss rate and a risk of worsening transplacental passage. The near pair here is cytomegalovirus, where amniocentesis does change counselling and is appropriate. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Parvovirus B19 infection)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Parvovirus B19 infection

explanation.summary: Parvovirus B19 causes erythema infectiosum in children and a self limiting arthropathy in adults, and around half of pregnant women are already immune, so establishing susceptibility with paired immunoglobulin M and G is the first step after an exposure. The virus infects erythroid progenitors, so the foetal consequence is aplastic anaemia that can progress to high output cardiac failure and hydrops, with the risk highest when infection occurs before 20 weeks and concentrated in the 8 to 12 weeks following maternal infection. Unlike cytomegalovirus and rubella, it does not cause a congenital malformation syndrome or late neurodevelopmental sequelae in survivors, which substantially changes the tone of counselling. The intervention that alters outcome is intrauterine transfusion for detected anaemia, and spontaneous resolution of mild hydrops also occurs, so surveillance rather than intervention is the initial response.
key_points: Immunoglobulin M positive with immunoglobulin G negative indicates very recent infection
Foetal risk is anaemia and hydrops rather than structural malformation
Risk is concentrated in the 8 to 12 weeks after maternal infection
Middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity detects anaemia non invasively
Intrauterine transfusion can reverse hydrops and is the effective intervention
explanation.pearls: Foetal hydrops from this infection can resolve spontaneously as the foetal marrow recovers, so a foetus with early hydrops and a peak systolic velocity below 1.5 multiples of the median is watched closely rather than transfused immediately.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Parvovirus B19 infection

subtopic_detail: Fever with diarrhoea and backache at thirty weeks after eating soft cheese and pre prepared salad with a negative urine dipstick
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar assessing a 33 year old woman at 30 weeks who has had two days of fever, muscle aches, headache and loose stools. She has no urinary frequency, no dysuria and no loin tenderness, and she has no cough or sore throat.

She tells you she has been careful with food but ate a soft cheese platter and a pre prepared supermarket salad at a family gathering five days ago. She looks flushed and unwell. Her uterus is soft and non tender with no contractions, and the cardiotocograph shows a baseline of 165 beats per minute with reduced variability that has not been present on previous traces. Her urine dipstick is negative for nitrites, leucocytes and protein.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 116 beats per minute, blood pressure 106/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 38.9 degrees Celsius, foetal heart rate 165 beats per minute
data_table.Examination: Flushed and unwell, chest clear on auscultation, abdomen soft with a non tender uterus, no renal angle tenderness, no rash, no neck stiffness
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 15.6 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), C reactive protein 96 mg/L (less than 5), urine dipstick negative for nitrites leucocytes and protein, cardiotocograph baseline 165 beats per minute with reduced variability and no decelerations, liver function tests within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Take blood cultures and start oral azithromycin pending the results
options.rationale: A macrolide is not reliable therapy for the organism suggested by this food history and illness pattern, and oral therapy is inadequate for a febrile bacteraemic pregnant woman with foetal compromise on the trace. Intravenous therapy is required while cultures are processed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Take blood cultures and start intravenous benzylpenicillin empirically
options.rationale: A febrile flu like illness with diarrhoea after eating high risk foods in the third trimester, with an unexplained foetal tachycardia, should be treated as listeriosis until blood cultures exclude it, and high dose intravenous penicillin or amoxicillin is the effective regimen. Empirical treatment is started before confirmation because delay is associated with foetal loss, preterm birth and neonatal sepsis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Take blood cultures and start oral cefalexin pending the culture result
options.rationale: Cephalosporins have no useful activity against this organism, which is intrinsically resistant to the entire class, so a reflex choice of cephalosporin for a febrile pregnant woman would leave the infection untreated. A negative urine dipstick also argues against the urinary source cefalexin would be chosen for. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Take a stool culture and withhold antibiotics pending the stool result
options.rationale: Stool culture is insensitive for this organism and the diagnosis is made on blood culture, so waiting for stool results both delays and misdirects the investigation. Withholding antibiotics in a bacteraemic pregnant woman with foetal tachycardia is unsafe. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Take blood cultures and start intravenous ceftriaxone empirically today
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone is a reasonable empirical choice for many infections in pregnancy but shares the class wide gap in activity against this organism. The near pair here is that ceftriaxone plus a penicillin would cover both possibilities, whereas ceftriaxone alone leaves the very diagnosis the food history suggests untreated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Listeriosis is rare but disproportionately affects pregnant women, in whom cell mediated immunity is relatively suppressed, and the maternal illness is often mild and non specific with fever, myalgia, headache and diarrhoea rather than a dramatic sepsis picture. The clue is usually the food history, since the organism grows at refrigeration temperatures and is associated with soft cheeses, pre prepared salads, deli meats, pate and smoked seafood, all of which are covered by Australian food safety advice in pregnancy. Diagnosis is by blood culture, because stool culture is insensitive and serology is not useful, and the laboratory should be told that listeriosis is suspected. The critical prescribing point is that the organism is intrinsically resistant to all cephalosporins, so the standard empirical cephalosporin chosen for a febrile pregnant woman will miss it, and high dose intravenous benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin is required.
key_points: Maternal illness is often mild and non specific despite serious foetal risk
The food history is frequently the only pointer to the diagnosis
Diagnosis is by blood culture, since stool culture is insensitive
The organism is intrinsically resistant to all cephalosporins
Unexplained foetal tachycardia may be the first sign of foetal infection
explanation.pearls: Australian food safety advice in pregnancy targets this organism specifically because it multiplies at refrigerator temperatures, which is why chilled ready to eat foods such as pre prepared salads, soft cheeses and cold deli meats are the recognised vehicles rather than food left unrefrigerated.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Routine antenatal assessment in the absence of pregnancy complications

subtopic_detail: Hirsutism and oligomenorrhoea with an early follicular 17 hydroxyprogesterone of 9 nmol/L in a twenty three year old
stem:
You are the gynaecologist seeing a 23 year old woman with coarse dark hair on her upper lip, chin and lower abdomen that she has been waxing since she was 15, and periods that come every six to ten weeks. She is not currently seeking pregnancy and takes no regular medication.

Her body mass index is 22 kg per square metre and there is no acanthosis nigricans, no abdominal striae and no proximal muscle weakness. Her voice is unchanged, her clitoris is of normal size and the hair growth has been slowly progressive since adolescence rather than appearing over months. An early follicular blood test taken at 8 in the morning shows a 17 hydroxyprogesterone of 9 nmol/L, with a mildly raised total testosterone and a normal prolactin.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 22 kg per square metre, modified Ferriman-Gallwey score 14 with terminal hair on the upper lip, chin, lower abdomen and thighs, no acanthosis nigricans, no striae, no proximal myopathy, normal clitoral size, no temporal balding
data_table.Investigations: Early follicular 17 hydroxyprogesterone 9 nmol/L taken at 0800 (less than 6), total testosterone mildly elevated, sex hormone binding globulin within normal limits, prolactin within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate mildly elevated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start the combined oral contraceptive pill and review her in six months
options.rationale: Combined hormonal contraception is appropriate treatment for hirsutism and cycle control once the cause is established, but starting it now suppresses the androgens and makes the diagnostic test uninterpretable for months. The diagnosis matters because it changes genetic counselling and fertility advice. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Assessment of hyperandrogenism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Assessment of hyperandrogenism

options.text: Start metformin and refer for lifestyle support, then review in six months
options.rationale: Metformin and lifestyle measures address insulin resistance, which is not suggested by a body mass index of 22 with no acanthosis nigricans, and they do not treat an adrenal enzyme defect. Assuming polycystic ovary syndrome without excluding its mimics is the anti pattern here. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Assessment of hyperandrogenism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Assessment of hyperandrogenism

options.text: Arrange a pelvic ultrasound to count antral follicles and then reassess
options.rationale: Polycystic ovarian morphology is common in young women and is frequently present in this condition as well, so the scan cannot distinguish between them. Ultrasound is also not required for the diagnosis of polycystic ovary syndrome when oligomenorrhoea and hyperandrogenism are both present. (Source: International evidence based guideline for polycystic ovary syndrome)
source_refs: International evidence based guideline for polycystic ovary syndrome

options.text: Arrange an adrenocorticotrophic hormone stimulation test before treatment
options.rationale: A basal early follicular 17 hydroxyprogesterone above about 6 nmol/L cannot distinguish a partial 21 hydroxylase deficiency from polycystic ovary syndrome, and the stimulated value is what separates them, with a marked rise after synthetic adrenocorticotrophic hormone confirming the enzyme defect. Confirming it matters because it changes reproductive counselling, since a partner who is a carrier creates a risk of a severely affected child. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Assessment of hyperandrogenism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Assessment of hyperandrogenism

options.text: Measure a twenty four hour urinary free cortisol and then reassess her
options.rationale: Cortisol excess is excluded clinically by the absence of striae, proximal myopathy, central obesity and hypertension, so screening for it has a very low pre test probability. The near pair here is that rapidly progressive virilisation with those physical signs would make cortisol and androgen secreting tumours the priority instead. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Assessment of hyperandrogenism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Assessment of hyperandrogenism

explanation.summary: Polycystic ovary syndrome is a diagnosis of exclusion, and the conditions that must be excluded before it is made are non-classical congenital adrenal hyperplasia, thyroid disease, hyperprolactinaemia and, where features suggest it, an androgen secreting tumour or cortisol excess. Non-classical 21 hydroxylase deficiency is the mimic that most often escapes detection, since it presents in adolescence or early adulthood with hirsutism, acne and irregular cycles that are clinically indistinguishable from the syndrome, and polycystic ovarian morphology is frequently present as well. An early follicular morning 17 hydroxyprogesterone is the screening test, and values above roughly 6 nmol/L require an adrenocorticotrophic hormone stimulation test, while values above about 30 nmol/L are diagnostic without stimulation. Rapid onset over months with virilisation, meaning voice change, clitoromegaly and temporal balding, shifts the priority to imaging for an androgen secreting tumour.
key_points: Polycystic ovary syndrome requires exclusion of its endocrine mimics
The screening test is 17 hydroxyprogesterone in the early follicular phase before 8 am
Stimulation testing separates a partial enzyme defect from the syndrome
Polycystic ovarian morphology does not distinguish between the two
Rapid virilisation suggests a tumour rather than either diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Diagnosing non-classical 21 hydroxylase deficiency changes preconception care rather than day to day treatment, because a woman with the condition whose partner carries a severe mutation has a risk of a child with the salt wasting classical form, so partner genotyping is offered before she conceives.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia: Assessment of hyperandrogenism
International evidence based guideline for polycystic ovary syndrome
BMJ Best Practice: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia

subtopic_detail: Screening for gestational diabetes at twenty six weeks two years after sleeve gastrectomy in a woman with post prandial dizziness
stem:
You are the obstetrician seeing a 34 year old woman at 26 weeks in her first pregnancy. She had a sleeve gastrectomy two years ago and her weight has been stable for the past year at a body mass index of 29 kg per square metre.

She tells you that if she eats anything sweet on an empty stomach she feels hot, shaky and light headed about twenty minutes later, and then washed out an hour or so after that. She takes the multivitamin, iron and vitamin B12 supplements prescribed by the bariatric service. Her booking glycated haemoglobin was 5.2 per cent, her foetal growth is on the 45th centile and her amniotic fluid volume is normal. She has been booked for a glucose tolerance test tomorrow morning and asks whether she should attend.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 29 kg per square metre, symphysis fundal height 26 cm consistent with dates, well healed laparoscopic port sites
data_table.Investigations: Booking glycated haemoglobin 5.2 per cent (less than 6.5), haemoglobin 118 g/L (115 to 155), ferritin 42 micrograms/L (30 to 200), vitamin B12 within normal limits, growth ultrasound at the 45th centile with normal amniotic fluid volume

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to screening her for gestational diabetes?

options.text: Arrange one week of fasting and post prandial capillary glucose monitoring
options.rationale: After sleeve gastrectomy the rapid delivery of a glucose load to the small bowel produces an exaggerated early peak followed by reactive hypoglycaemia, so the test both provokes distressing symptoms and yields values that cannot be interpreted against thresholds derived from an intact stomach. A week of home capillary glucose profiles measures her actual glycaemic exposure across normal meals and is the recommended alternative in this group. (Source: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy)
source_refs: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy

options.text: Proceed with the standard 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 26 weeks
options.rationale: The standard load is exactly what provokes dumping and reactive hypoglycaemia after this operation, and the resulting curve is uninterpretable because the diagnostic thresholds assume normal gastric emptying. Her description of symptoms after sweet food on an empty stomach predicts that response. (Source: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy)
source_refs: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy

options.text: Measure glycated haemoglobin alone and repeat the measurement at 32 weeks
options.rationale: Glycated haemoglobin is lowered in pregnancy by increased red cell turnover and is further distorted by the iron deficiency common after bariatric surgery, so it is insensitive for gestational hyperglycaemia. It is useful at booking to detect pre existing diabetes rather than to screen in the third trimester. (Source: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy)
source_refs: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy

options.text: Measure a random plasma glucose alone and repeat the test at 32 weeks
options.rationale: A single unstandardised value has poor sensitivity and cannot characterise the fasting and post prandial pattern that determines whether treatment is needed. It would miss the woman whose fasting values are normal but whose post prandial excursions are not. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Gestational diabetes)

options.text: Omit screening because bariatric surgery removes the risk of diabetes
options.rationale: Bariatric surgery reduces but does not abolish the risk, and these women remain more likely than the general obstetric population to develop hyperglycaemia in pregnancy. The near pair here is that the operation changes how she is screened, not whether she is screened. (Source: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy)
source_refs: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy

explanation.summary: Pregnancy after bariatric surgery is increasingly common and brings a distinct set of considerations, including micronutrient deficiency, a smaller for gestational age tendency, and an altered response to a glucose load. After a sleeve gastrectomy or a bypass, gastric emptying is accelerated, so a 75 g drink produces an early exaggerated glucose peak, a brisk insulin response and then symptomatic hypoglycaemia at two hours, a pattern that is both unpleasant and impossible to score against standard diagnostic thresholds. Australian practice in this group is to substitute a week of capillary glucose monitoring, using the same fasting and post prandial targets that would be applied to treat gestational diabetes. Nutritional surveillance runs alongside, since iron, vitamin B12, folate and fat soluble vitamin deficiencies are common and affect both the woman and the foetus.
key_points: Accelerated gastric emptying makes the standard glucose load uninterpretable
Dumping with reactive hypoglycaemia is provoked by the test itself
Capillary glucose profiles over a week are the recommended substitute
Glycated haemoglobin is unreliable in pregnancy and after bariatric surgery
The operation changes how screening is done rather than whether it is done
explanation.pearls: Women who have had a bypass rather than a sleeve are additionally at risk of internal herniation as the uterus enlarges, so any pregnant woman with previous bariatric surgery and persistent or severe abdominal pain needs surgical assessment rather than reassurance that it is a pregnancy symptom.

sources.label: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy
RANZCOG: Management of obesity in pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Toxoplasma seroconversion detected at eleven weeks on repeat serology with low avidity immunoglobulin G
stem:
You are the obstetrician seeing a 29 year old woman at 11 weeks in her first pregnancy. She had serology taken privately before conception that was negative for toxoplasma immunoglobulin G, and a repeat panel taken last week because of a two week illness with tender neck glands and fatigue.

She keeps two cats and has been emptying the litter tray herself, and she gardens without gloves. The repeat serology is immunoglobulin M positive and immunoglobulin G positive with a low avidity index, and the reference laboratory reports this as consistent with infection acquired within the last three months. She feels well now. Ultrasound today shows a structurally normal foetus with a crown rump length consistent with dates.

data_table.Examination: Small mobile non tender posterior cervical lymph nodes, no rash, no hepatosplenomegaly, uterus consistent with dates
data_table.Investigations: Preconception toxoplasma immunoglobulin G negative, current toxoplasma immunoglobulin M positive and immunoglobulin G positive with a low avidity index, full blood count within normal limits, ultrasound reports a structurally normal foetus with crown rump length consistent with dates

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Start oral azithromycin and arrange monthly ultrasound until delivery
options.rationale: Azithromycin has some activity against the organism but is not the agent used to reduce vertical transmission, and monthly imaging is less intensive than the surveillance an infected pregnancy requires. Choosing an unproven agent forfeits the benefit of the established one. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Start pyrimethamine with sulfadiazine and folinic acid immediately now
options.rationale: This combination is used when foetal infection has been confirmed, and pyrimethamine is a folate antagonist that is avoided in the first trimester because of teratogenicity. Giving it before the foetal status is known exposes the foetus to the drug without evidence that it is infected. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Offer termination of pregnancy given the risk of congenital infection
options.rationale: Transmission risk at 11 weeks is low, around 5 to 10 per cent, and most infected pregnancies proceed to a normal outcome, particularly with treatment. Offering termination before the foetal status is even established misrepresents the prognosis. (Source: RANZCOG: Toxoplasmosis in pregnancy)

options.text: Reassure and continue routine care since maternal infection is benign
options.rationale: Maternal illness is indeed mild or silent, but that says nothing about the foetal consequences, which include chorioretinitis, intracranial calcification and hydrocephalus when transmission occurs early. The near pair here is that seroconversion before conception genuinely does not require action, whereas seroconversion during pregnancy does. (Source: RANZCOG: Toxoplasmosis in pregnancy)

options.text: Start spiramycin and arrange amniocentesis for nucleic acid testing
options.rationale: Spiramycin concentrates in the placenta and is started immediately to reduce transmission across it, without crossing to treat the foetus, while amniocentesis for nucleic acid amplification testing from 18 weeks and at least four weeks after seroconversion establishes whether transmission has occurred. That result determines whether she continues spiramycin or switches to the regimen that treats established foetal infection. (Source: RANZCOG: Toxoplasmosis in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Australia does not screen routinely for toxoplasma in pregnancy, so the diagnosis is usually made after a clinically suspicious illness or an incidental test, and interpreting the serology is the first difficulty because immunoglobulin M persists for months to years after infection. Avidity testing resolves this, since low avidity immunoglobulin G indicates recent infection while high avidity effectively excludes infection within the preceding three to four months, and a documented preconception negative result makes the timing unambiguous as it does here. The risk of transmission rises through pregnancy while the severity of foetal disease falls, so early infection is uncommon but damaging and late infection is common but usually mild or subclinical. Management follows a two branch algorithm, with spiramycin given to reduce transmission while the foetal status is determined, then either continued or replaced by pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine and folinic acid if foetal infection is confirmed.
key_points: Immunoglobulin M persists long after infection and cannot date it alone
Low avidity immunoglobulin G indicates infection within the last three to four months
Transmission risk rises with gestation while severity of foetal disease falls
Spiramycin reduces transmission but does not cross to treat the foetus
Amniocentesis result determines which treatment branch is followed
explanation.pearls: Amniocentesis for toxoplasma nucleic acid testing should be delayed until at least 18 weeks and at least four weeks after the estimated time of maternal infection, because sampling earlier produces false negatives before the organism has crossed the placenta in detectable amounts.
